title: Steinitz, the first world champion
summary: 1886: in the first official world championship match, Steinitz blockades an isolated pawn and slowly squeezes Zukertort.

steps.title: The first title match
steps.text: In 1886 Wilhelm Steinitz and Johannes Zukertort played a match in the United States that counts as the first official world championship. Steinitz won it and became the first world champion. He taught something new: before you attack, collect small advantages, like a weak pawn or a strong square. In this game he has Black. You play his side.
steps.narration: 1886, the first official world championship match. Wilhelm Steinitz believed in small advantages: a weak pawn here, a strong square there. Watch them add up. You play Black, as Steinitz.

steps.title: Zukertort – Steinitz, World Championship 1886
steps.text: Early on, White's d-pawn becomes isolated: it has no pawn neighbours to protect it. Steinitz parks a knight in front of it, trades pieces, and waits. Zukertort attacks on the kingside, and Steinitz is ready. The game stops at Steinitz's key moves.
steps.narration: White ends up with a lonely pawn on d4. Steinitz blocks it, presses it, and waits for his chance. Find his key moves.

notes.text: 7.exd4: White's d-pawn now stands alone, with no white pawns on the c- or e-files to protect it. That is an isolated pawn.
11...Nbd5: a knight lands right in front of the isolated pawn. No white pawn can ever chase it from d5.
18.bxc3: White's pawns on c3 and d4 now stand together, but both are targets.
19...Nd5: the other knight takes over the blockade square.
22.c4: White's c- and d-pawns stand side by side with no neighbours. Strong if they can advance, weak if they get attacked.
25.Rh3: Zukertort swings a rook toward Black's king and starts an attack.
30...f5: Steinitz gains space on the kingside and prepares a fine square for his bishop on e4.
33.c5: White pushes a pawn to hit the queen. It looks strong, but there is a tactic.
38...Qxe4: Black is up material, White's knight on d1 is tied up, and Zukertort resigned.

guesses.prompt: White just took your knight on d5. Which piece should take back?
guesses.hint: Taking with the pawn would give you an isolated pawn of your own. Keep the pressure on d4.
guesses.why: 21...Rxd5! The rook takes back and attacks d4 at once. Taking with the e-pawn would have blocked the d-file and left Black with a lonely pawn of his own.

guesses.prompt: Zukertort's rook has reached g6. Find a strong central square for your bishop.
guesses.hint: Look for a square where the bishop attacks the white queen and is protected by a pawn.
guesses.why: 31...Be4! The bishop hits the queen on d3 and takes a fine central post, protected by the f5 pawn. White's attack runs out of steam.

guesses.prompt: 33.c5 attacks your queen. Do not move her. Find something stronger.
guesses.hint: If White's d-pawn captures on c5, what does your queen see down the d-file?
guesses.why: 33...Rxc5! The d4 pawn cannot take back: it is pinned, because after the pawn takes, the queen would capture the rook on d2. Steinitz wins the pawn he had been pressing all game.

guesses.prompt: White took on e6. Your rook can join the attack with check. How?
guesses.hint: White's back rank has no defenders.
guesses.why: 34...Rc1+! The rook invades with check, and the knight has to block on d1, where it gets stuck.

steps.title: Small advantages add up
steps.text: Steinitz never rushed at the king in this game. He blocked the lonely d-pawn with a knight, traded pieces, and kept pressing until White's pawns cracked. That was his big idea: collect small advantages, and the winning tactics will show up by themselves.
steps.narration: No wild attack. Steinitz blocked the weak pawn, kept pressing, and the tactics came on their own. That is how the first world champion played.

steps.title: Against the isolated pawn
steps.question: White has an isolated pawn on d4. Where does Black want a piece?

options.text: On d5, right in front of the pawn
options.why: Yes. A piece on d5 stops the pawn from moving, and no white pawn can chase it away.

options.text: On d8, far behind its own pawns
options.why: Too passive. From d8 the piece does nothing to stop the pawn or to use the square in front of it.

options.text: Anywhere, as long as it attacks the king
options.why: Steinitz taught the opposite: work on the weaknesses first, and attack later.

steps.narration: One question: where do you want a piece against an isolated pawn?
